title: Two corners off the board
hook: Take two corners off a 4 by 4 board. Can dominoes still cover the rest?

knows: a domino covers two neighbouring squares
doesNotKnow: that counting colours can prove a tiling impossible without trying every arrangement

misconception: Remove two squares from a board with an even number of squares and the rest can always be covered by dominoes, if you try hard enough.
objective: The learner can say that a 4 by 4 board without two opposite corners cannot be covered by 7 dominoes, because every domino covers one dark and one light square and the board has 6 dark and 8 light, and that this count rules out every arrangement without trying them.

claims.text: Every domino on a chequered board covers one dark and one light square, whichever way it lies.
claims.source: Neighbouring squares (r, c) and (r, c+1) or (r+1, c) differ by 1 in r + c, so one has r + c even (dark) and the other odd (light). Stage: isDark(r, c) = (r + c) even in Demo.tsx; every drawn domino is checked to be two neighbouring squares at module load.

claims.text: A 4 by 4 board without two opposite corners ((0,0) and (3,3), both dark) has 6 dark and 8 light squares, so at most 6 dominoes fit and every best try leaves 2 light squares; it has no domino tiling, and counting colours shows this without trying every arrangement. Without two corners of one row ((0,0) and (0,3)) it has 7 dark and 7 light and 12 tilings. The stage draws fixed tries: on the opposite-corner board 6 dominoes leaving (2,3) and (3,2), then (0,3) and (3,0), then (0,1) and (1,0); on the one-row board three of its 12 tilings (every domino horizontal; the bottom two rows as four vertical dominoes; four vertical and three horizontal dominoes).
claims.source: company/domains/briefs/checks/math-wave-j-check.mjs label D4 (opposite: dark 6, light 8, tilings 0; sameRow: dark 7, light 7, tilings 12). Maximum matching by brute force over all domino sets: 6 on the opposite-corner board (154 maximum placements). The fixed tries are listed in BOARDS in Demo.tsx; the readout is counted from the drawn board.

claims.text: An 8 by 8 chessboard without two opposite corners has 30 dark and 32 light squares, so 31 dominoes cannot cover it. Recall: a 6 by 6 board without two squares of the same colour has 16 of one colour and 18 of the other, so 17 dominoes cannot cover it.
claims.source: company/domains/briefs/checks/math-wave-j-check.mjs label D4 (8x8 opp: [30, 32]). Opposite corners (0,0) and (7,7) both have r + c even, so both are the same colour; 32 - 2 = 30. Recall: 6 by 6 has 18 of each colour; removing two of one colour leaves 16 and 18; with claim c1, 17 dominoes need 17 of each.

recall.question: A 6 by 6 chequered board loses two squares of the same colour. 34 squares are left. Can 17 dominoes cover them exactly?
options: Only if the two squares are corners
recall.why: Each domino covers one dark and one light square, but the board now has 16 of one colour and 18 of the other, so 17 dominoes can never fit.
